screeningScope: Full-text source, eligibility, taxonomy, and synthesis-readiness review of Rehabilitation & Return to Sport queue positions 17-94. Drafted by Claude Haiku 5.5 and claim-audited against source text by Claude Opus 5.5 (docs/haiku-calibration/).

decisionDefinitions.INCLUDE: Eligible for evidence extraction and synthesis after full-text review.
decisionDefinitions.DEGRADED: A required source or verification element was unavailable.

records.sourceFile: Running speed increases plantar load more than per cent body weight on an AlterG® treadmill.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Laboratory study in 20 injury-free male experienced runners who ran on an AlterG treadmill at 6 to 16 km/h and 50 to 100% indicated bodyweight (36 conditions), with peak plantar force measured by Pedar-X in-shoe insoles. Peak force ranged from 1.02 BW (6 km/h, 50% BW) to 2.31 BW (16 km/h, 100% BW). In Table 1, raising speed from 6 to 16 km/h at fixed bodyweight increased peak force by about 0.75 to 1.10 BW, against about 0.19 to 0.56 BW for raising bodyweight from 50 to 100% at fixed speed.
records.limitations: Only healthy male runners were tested, so the values do not show how injured or female athletes respond. In-shoe sensors sampled at 100 Hz capture only the vertical force, so true peaks and shear loads may be missed.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read Table 1 as a fixed rehabilitation prescription, when the authors present it as a reference that still needs clinical judgement for each athlete.

changes: evidenceSummary/findings: reported abstract/Table 2 relative values (0.74-0.91 vs 0.19-0.31 BW) as absolute increases -> Table 1 absolute differences, speed about 0.75-1.10 BW and bodyweight about 0.19-0.56 BW ('a minimum of 0.75BW increase ... to a maximum of 1.10BW'; 'maximum of 0.54BW (for the 14 km/hr condition)')
limitations: added note on abstract/Table 2 versus Table 1 discrepancy
tldr: 'Use speed as the main step in progression' could push large load jumps -> speed is the big step, bodyweight the small step (text: initial small increases come from stepping indicated BW)
verification.residualConcerns: Abstract, Table 2 and the discussion give inconsistent bodyweight-effect ranges (0.31, 0.329, 0.54 BW); Table 1 values were used.

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Controlled laboratory study in 24 people 6 to 12 months after ACL reconstruction (15 female, 9 male), walking on a split-belt treadmill with the operated-leg belt set at 30% to 170% of 1.1 m/s in eight randomised 5-minute conditions. Faster operated-leg speeds increased early-stance knee moments and vertical loads, while slower speeds lowered early peaks and raised midstance loading. The authors report a dose-response relationship between decoupling speed and knee and limb loading.
records.limitations: The study examines acute single-session effects with 2-minute washouts, so aftereffects and training effects were not tested. Participants were not described as athletes, and they did not show the baseline loading asymmetry the authors expected.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff may read the split-belt result as a proven way to correct underloading after ACL reconstruction, when the study measured only acute gait changes during one treadmill session.

changes: paper.citation: online-first page range '2025:1-9' with header 'Vol. XX, No. X, XXXX' treated as placeholder -> removed pages
paper.findings: clarified the early-stance changes were bilateral and that second peak vGRF fitted a fourth-order polynomial ('fits best with a fourth-order polynomial')

records.sourceFile: Self-Reported Fear Predicts              Functional Performance and Second ACL Injury After ACL       Reconstruction     and    Return to Sport- A Pilot Study.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Prospective cohort pilot of 40 patients (ages 10 to 25, mean 16.2) cleared for return to sport after primary ACL reconstruction, who completed the TSK-11 fear questionnaire, the Marx activity scale, single-leg hop tests and isometric quadriceps strength, and were followed for 24 months. Patients with TSK-11 of 17 or more (n = 19) more often had low Marx activity (73.7% vs 42.9%), single-leg hop for distance limb symmetry of 95% or less (55.6% vs 15%) and quadriceps LSI of 90% or less (50% vs 14.3%) than low-fear patients. Fifteen patients (37.5%) had a second ACL injury, and ipsilateral injury was linked to higher TSK-11 scores (19.8 vs 16.4, P = 0.03).
records.limitations: The study is a 40-patient pilot at one institution, with 8 ipsilateral and 7 contralateral second injuries, so the injury estimates are very imprecise. The activity CI crosses 1 (OR 3.73, 95% CI 0.98 to 14.23), the cut-offs were chosen from clinical convention, and the associations are not causal.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could treat the TSK-11 as a validated discharge gate that predicts reinjury, when this pilot found associations in 40 patients and the authors say it needs further study before it is used as a criterion.

changes: findings and evidenceSummary: 'hop LSI' -> single-leg hop for distance only; added that other hop tests showed no association ('No associations between fear and other functional hop tests were identified')
abstract and findings: RR 13.0 for 'second ACL tear' -> ipsilateral second ACL tear ('13 times ... more likely to suffer an ipsilateral second ACL tear')
limitations: added abstract vs body conflict on follow-up ('tracked for 12 months' vs 'tracked for 24 months after RTS')
athleteDev: 'less likely to return to high activity levels' implied a future outcome -> activity was measured at clearance and the association was not significant (OR 3.73, 95% CI 0.98-14.23)
verification.residualConcerns: Return-to-sport clearance topic; the RR 13.0 (95% CI 2.1 to 81.0) rests on 8 ipsilateral injuries. Citation has no volume or pages because only placeholders ('vol. XX no. X') are printed.

records.sourceFile: Sensorimotor Dysfunction Following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury (Part 1) What Is It - How Can Clinicians Assess It.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Clinical commentary that works as a narrative clinical review, with no described search method, summarising evidence on sensorimotor changes after ACL injury and proposing clinic-based tests. The authors describe dysfunction across afferent pathways (pain, swelling, reduced proprioception, increased visual-motor reliance and cortical processing) and efferent pathways (reduced motor cortex and corticospinal excitability, spinal reflex excitability reduced acutely then increased chronically). They recommend joint position sense, pain, effusion, visual-motor reliance and processing, strength and surface EMG activation tests.
records.limitations: No search or selection method is described, and several recommendations, retest intervals and the stepdown visual-reliance test rest on the authors' clinical practice and unpublished reliability data. The article reports no new study and does not link any test to reinjury.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could treat the proposed test battery and its retest intervals as a validated reinjury screen, when the authors state that visual-motor tests still need normative values and research on whether they relate to reinjury.

changes: decision: EXCLUDE (b) commentary -> INCLUDE as Narrative Review. The article is a structured clinical review of evidence (Background, Clinical question, Key results, Clinical application, three evidence tables, Key Points, about 105 references); 'no search method described' defines a Narrative Review, which INSTRUCTIONS lists as eligible, not an exclusion ('This clinical commentary outlines sensorimotor changes ... and proposes evidence-based methods')
all taxonomy, summary and paper fields: null -> written from the text
paper.doi: set to 10.2519/jospt.2025.12725 from the article header ('https://doi.org/10.2519/https://doi.org/10.2519/jospt.2025.12725')
verification.residualConcerns: The article labels itself a 'clinical commentary'; a reviewer may decide that JOSPT clinical commentaries fall under exclusion (b) instead. The printed DOI string is duplicated in the header and was cleaned to the jospt.2025.12725 suffix. Advance publication, so no volume or pages.

records.sourceFile: Sensorimotor Dysfunction Following Anterior Cruciate Ligament Injury (Part 2) - How Can Clinicians Rehabilitate It.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Clinical commentary that works as a narrative clinical review, with no described search method, of rehabilitation methods for sensorimotor dysfunction after ACL injury and reconstruction. The authors set two priorities: restoring peripheral and central efferent function (cryotherapy, TENS, high-intensity strength training, NMES, surface EMG biofeedback) and improving somatosensory function while reducing visual-motor reliance (proprioceptive training progressed in complexity).
records.limitations: No search or selection method is described, several dosages come from other populations or the authors' practice, and the authors state there is no prospective research on whether proprioceptive training reduces visual-motor reliance. The article reports no new study.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the dosing guidance (for example TENS, NMES and stroboscopic schedules) as proven for ACLR sensorimotor outcomes, when several doses are practice-based or extrapolated and the effect of proprioceptive training after ACLR has not been studied.

changes: decision: EXCLUDE (b) commentary -> INCLUDE as Narrative Review. The article is a structured clinical review of evidence (Background, Clinical question, Key results, Clinical application, Key Points, about 65 references); 'no search method described' defines a Narrative Review, which INSTRUCTIONS lists as eligible ('The aim of this clinical commentary is to review methods that may improve rehabilitation')
all taxonomy, summary and paper fields: null -> written from the text
paper.doi: set to 10.2519/jospt.2025.12726 from the article header
verification.residualConcerns: The article labels itself a 'clinical commentary'; a reviewer may decide that JOSPT clinical commentaries fall under exclusion (b) instead. Mentions pain medication (nerve blocks, NSAIDs), cryotherapy and TENS dosing. Advance publication, so no volume or pages.

records.sourceFile: Should return to sport be delayed until 2 years after      ACL reconstruction - Biological and functional      considerations.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Narrative clinical review of biological (bone bruise, graft maturation, sensory), functional (neuromuscular control, quadriceps and hamstring strength, hop tests) and surgical/rehabilitation studies after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction (ACLR), written as a Sports Medicine review article with no described search method. The authors argue that young, active athletes do not reach baseline joint health and function until about two years after ACLR, and that the second-injury risk is highest in the first two years, with nearly one in three of the younger cohort re-injured within that period.
records.limitations: The review uses no described search or selection method, so the evidence base cannot be checked for completeness. Its central recommendation, a two-year delay, is argued from mechanisms and cohort studies, and the authors present it as a postulate rather than a tested intervention.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read a two-year minimum as an evidence-based rule for every athlete, when the paper presents it as a postulate that no trial has tested and does not give criteria for individual decisions.

changes: paper.abstract: 'They conclude that delaying ... would substantially reduce' -> 'They postulate ... would significantly reduce' ('We postulate that delay in returning to sports for nearly 2 years will significantly reduce the incidence of second ACL injuries')
synthesisCaution: 'a postulate to be tested' -> 'a postulate that no trial has tested' (the text never says the authors call for testing it)

paper.practicalImplications: 'the authors frame it as a hypothesis to test' -> 'the delay is the authors' postulate and has not been tested as an intervention' (the conclusion states the delay 'will restore knee joint homeostasis and significantly reduce the risk')
verification.residualConcerns: The paper is headed 'REVIEW ARTICLE' but twice calls itself a 'current opinion article'; INCLUDE as a narrative review is defensible but a reviewer may want to confirm. Return-to-sport timing paper, so clinically sensitive.

records.sourceFile: Similar Isokinetic Strength Preinjury and at Return to Sport after Hamstring Injury.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: Pooled analysis of 41 professional male soccer players with an MRI-confirmed hamstring injury, drawn from two single-site randomized trials at Aspetar in Qatar. Isokinetic strength of the injured limb at return to sport was compared with each player's own pre-injury screening values, and side-to-side differences were compared at both time points. The injured limb averaged over 95% of pre-injury strength, with 63.4% of players showing a >10% deficit and 57.9% a >10% surplus in at least one of five variables at return to sport, similar to pre-injury patterns.
records.limitations: This observational pooled analysis covers 41 players from one clinical setting, includes only grade I and II injuries, and has incomplete re-injury data, so it cannot test whether isokinetic cut-offs predict re-injury. Results may not apply to other sports, female players or MRI-negative injuries.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could read the 10% deficit figure as proof that many players are still weak at return, but similar proportions also differ from their own pre-injury values, and the authors argue these differences fall within test variability.

changes: paper.methods: omitted the eccentric test -> added eccentric knee extension at 60 deg/s ("five repetitions of eccentric knee extension at 60 deg/s")
paper.tldr: 10% cut-off "did not separate players well" (not tested) -> a >10% difference was as common pre-injury as at return ("even observed in a similar proportion of players pre-injury")

paper.practicalImplications and athleteDev: claimed own pre-injury baseline is the better reference than the uninjured side, which the paper does not show -> interpret differences against test variability ("minimal detectable change in peak torque for all these measures is greater than 20%"; strength "varies by 15% from one pre-season to the next")

records.sourceFile: Sport-related structural brain injury and return to play - Systematic review and expert insight.pdf

sourceVerification.doiVerification: DOI printed in the local PDF text.

records.evidenceSummary: PRISMA-based systematic review of PubMed records on sport-related structural brain injury from 2012 onward: 241 records screened and 27 studies included, almost all case reports or series, of which only 12 athletes from 9 articles had return-to-play information. A survey of 31 of 32 invited sports neurosurgeons (96.9%) found that 12 (38.7%) would not operate on an acute, asymptomatic structural injury, and most allowed return to high-contact sport at 6 to 12 months after resolved hemorrhage.
records.limitations: The systematic review yields 27 studies, almost all of them case reports with level 4 evidence, and the survey reflects opinion from one specialist group, 71% of whom were US-based. A single reviewer screened records with senior verification, and the protocol was not registered.
records.synthesisCaution: Staff could treat the expert survey percentages, such as 6 to 12 months before return to high-contact sport, as an evidence-based return timeline, when they rest on 12 athletes' case reports and surgeon opinion, and the authors describe the responses as heterogeneous.

verification.residualConcerns: Return-to-play after structural brain injury is clinically sensitive. The printed regression (beta -0.58, 95% CI -0.111 to -0.005) is internally inconsistent in the source and is flagged in limitations.
